You can’t be high at that level all the time — it will actually turn into psychosis if you try. Those big bursts are what some of us go after. Gambling is one of those. It helped me understand I was bipolar. I got that diagnosis at one point, and I had to become the master of my dopamine as well, because I realized if I come up, I will go down. The trick wasn’t to try to change it and stay up. The trick was to realize when I was down, there was some work to do, some healing to do, and not just try to get back up — but allow myself to find that natural middle path in living. That was a big lesson. The other one is with endorphins — that’s where the love addict comes in. Sugar is the chemical or physical fix with endorphins, but on the emotional level it’s typically we’re seeking love. For a lot of us that’s romantic love, or some kind of belonging or security — that warm, fuzzy thing. And it’s not necessarily wrong. One of the things I found is what I call the spiral. The spiral includes things you want to do abstinence with on the outside — heroin is probably not a good idea on the endorphin continuum. You’re going to let that go. The next layer inward is moderation. I had to find a way to do moderation with this romantic craving. You get into the honeymoon and you want to stay there, and then it fluctuates. Some of that is moving past the addictive nature of love and into the third part of the cycle, which is attainment. Attainment is doing the work to have longer-term real solutions. In a relationship it’s not just “we love the honeymoon and then it gets hard — do we stay or do we go?” With the attainment part, it closes that gap, that inner hole which is really what we’re trying to fill, to a solution that’s more solid — a deeper love, a more complete sense of self. It could be self-love. You start getting into that center with that. Jacob: With these cycles, what are we trying to complete with these cycles ideally? What is it that we’re trying to get?

chapters.chapter_title: Jail curriculum / Yom Kippur light shaft / at-one-ment
chapters.excerpt: Cristine: It is a healing — an inner healing. I actually developed this spiral model when I was working in a jail. I took my recovery and started creating a curriculum with these concepts as a substance abuse counselor. I was teaching this, creating this, as I was working with inmates. Some of them told me they had even done this attainment thing. They’d say, “We did twelve years sober doing the AA thing,” and some of the attainment things are self-help programs or religious commitments or health and wellness commitments — things you’re probably not going to get addicted to, like going to the gym, or education. They were doing all these things right and they still relapsed. I took it as: this is the challenge. I had twenty years clean by the time I was teaching this, so I felt pretty stable, but there were areas of my life, like relationships, that I hadn’t figured out.

What’s interesting is I was on this spiritual journey — I was studying Kabbalah — and it happened to be the moment of Yom Kippur. Yom Kippur in the Jewish tradition starts at sundown and is a 24-hour Day of Atonement. If you look at that word, atonement is “at-one-ment.” It’s a devotion after Rosh Hashanah. You’ve done ten days of deep diving, excavating your past year and where you could improve. This 24 hours, people typically dress in white, they fast, they don’t work or engage in regular life stuff — they just spend that 24 hours in divine connection. I got home and realized, “Okay, well I guess I don’t know what this means, but I choose this.” I was lying on my couch and the sun went down. I remember there was this light — it almost entered like a shaft through the top of my head and poured through. It felt like my spine, from head to toe. I felt light enter me. And that was the solution. The solution of this spiral is at this center: really, all that matters is that you are whole and complete through a divine connection, and you bring your whole self to it. Jacob: Can I ask — I’m not sure what language you typically use for this now — do you call this a Kundalini awakening? Obviously spiritual awakening is terminology you’ve used, but have you dove into Kundalini?

chapters.chapter_title: Kundalini as vital-body tool (chakras, meridians, aura)
chapters.excerpt: Cristine: I have. I love Kundalini. Kundalini was very supportive. There was a phase in my life where my healing journey was very much influenced by it. My experience with that, though, is that the Kundalini was more about making corrections in my vital body. The vital body contains the chakras, meridians, and your aura field. That’s a layer of us that is very much neglected by Western medicine, but important in influencing the physical self and connected to the quantum self. So that’s where I would place Kundalini — a very effective vital body tool and process to clear and strengthen the vital body. Jacob: When you had your first kind of initial awakening… have you always had some sort of spiritual side to you? Did you grow up in a religion? Were you always spiritual, or was this kind of a later-in-life awakening?

chapters.chapter_title: Yearning for Freedom / cocaine phase / entity attachment
chapters.excerpt: Cristine: That’s a great question. I grew up in a religion, Christian-based, and I followed as much as I could with it. But like I just shared, my chemistry was not working, and religion didn’t fix it. So I left religion in my path with substance use. Here’s what’s kind of cool — and I’m going to release my recovery story, so I don’t want to give it all away because that’s going to come out. It’s called Yearning for Freedom. In my late teens and early young adult life, I just wanted freedom from the guilt, because that is one of the things that happens with someone who’s got a religious influence and is fighting against it or steering away from it. I wanted freedom from guilt, but I also wanted freedom from pain and suffering. I just thought if I could just find this, it’s got to be out there.

There was a moment when I had used this drug for about eight months or so and still could kind of take it or leave it — I could still do life and then wait for the weekend. But there was a night I remember very specifically. I was with a couple people and we were using, and a friend came to the door. This friend had been bubbly, energetic. She didn’t have depression like I dealt with… until we opened the door that night and her whole demeanor was different. Her vibration was different. Even then I could sense, “What happened?” She’d come back from a funeral — a friend of hers who had overdosed — and she just couldn’t shake it. She came over and joined the party, and I remember that almost in an instant I’d gone from the freedom I had with this drug to being controlled by it. Theoretically — and this is just me looking back — I believe the person who overdosed came with her and walked through the door. So this entity, this earthbound essence, attached to me. After that point in time I couldn’t say no. I didn’t have power over what was going on. I started losing weight. I started experiencing all the late-stage consequences of my use. That’s my theory. People may or may not get that. There’s actually a book that coincides with this called Return from Tomorrow. Richie is the name of the author. He talks about his near-death experience where he was moving in and out. He stepped into a bar and watched people sitting around the bar, but there were also earthbounds sitting around the bar with them, waiting for them to drink to a certain point, and then it was like they kind of unzipped them and entered to vicariously continue to have that experience. Isn’t that interesting? Jacob: That’s a very interesting way to look at it. I feel like it coincides with my experience as well — back in my days of drinking and partying and nights of cocaine. So what do you think that is? Do you see that as a positive way of addressing these things that people are dealing with? How can you spot it? If someone comes to you nowadays and maybe they have one of these entities hanging over them… what’s your approach if you deem that’s the case? How can we shake off these entities?

chapters.chapter_title: Perverse energy / generational clearing / Quantum University
chapters.excerpt: Cristine: This is actually where we start talking quantum things. In Quantum University they refer to this as perverse energy. You’re working at the spiritual level. Sometimes it’s generational. I’ve had clients who are affected by something that’s always been there. As we tune into that — and I use a lot of intuition with this — sometimes I’ll just know it’s an ancestor, like a great-grandfather or grandmother. I’ll say certain things and they’ll be like, “Oh yeah, I’ve heard that — my mom’s mom had depression,” or whatever. Sometimes I’m actually doing therapy on both. We invite them to stay and experience the healing. That’s quantum stuff. Kundalini is really interesting when you say that. My first Kundalini session was actually geared toward addiction release. The series was done by a gentleman who was using it for addiction recovery as well. I remember starting the process and experiencing my grandfather.

chapters.chapter_title: EFT (Gary Craig) → Zero Point Meridian / vs EMDR
chapters.excerpt: Cristine: Yes. EFT is the tapping technique — Emotional Freedom Technique. I started training in 2002–2003 when Gary Craig was actually doing his program. I went through all of his basic and all of his advanced. I loved it. I was in a career at the time where I couldn’t use it, and it inspired me or motivated me to get into private practice so I could have the freedom to use it with clients. As I was using that, I started developing very unique adaptations. Then with my training with Quantum University, I brought in accessing the zero point field and doing things to clear at the quantum level. So it became Zero Point Meridian — that’s what it’s called now, ZPM. Yes, I absolutely use that. In the case I described, a woman comes to my office and we figure out she’s carrying something that’s not even just hers.

chapters.chapter_title: Mental-body chaos / neutrality / “neutral game”
chapters.excerpt: Cristine: Perfect. We’re stepping right into the mental body. This is so interesting, and I hope people grab the Four Bodies, Four Medicines ebook to really explore this too. The example I use in there is: if we try to use the mind to correct the mind, we can get just a lot of chaos going on. It’s trying to go back and forth between positive thinking and negative thinking. “Oh, there I am doing negative thinking,” and then the judge comes in: “You shouldn’t be negative thinking.” So we have that voice, and then “You better be positive thinking,” and we have that voice. Just a lot of chaos. The solution I found for that is it goes back to zero. It’s actually neutrality. Neutrality has the option of not charging your thoughts with anything. I like playing the neutral game.

I like playing the neutral game. The neutral game is a way to bring the mind to the present moment with zero emotion — just neutral state, present moment. If I’m playing the game in my setting right here, I’m going to say: “Okay, there is a clock in front of me.” I can give the time. I can look around and see there are four frames on my wall. My chair is black. Then I can go into auditory senses: I hear some white noise… I might see something out the window. You’re bringing yourself back to “Oh, I can feel.” If I put my toes on the ground, I can feel my chair protector. I can feel the texture of my chair. You have to slow down to be able to identify the experience, and you avoid qualifiers or adjectives that add emotion to it. The goal is just: there are four drawers. The water bottle is blue. I smell… You can do it in your room. You can do it while you’re driving. A lot of times when I was driving and had a commute, I’d go into some headspace. Just practicing this: sky is blue, there’s a white car in front of me, turn off the radio, and just be in the silence. The trick is you’re actually changing your neural pathways with it — like a mindfulness exercise, basically. Jacob: I think it helps people really notice, because when you start to stack on a few of these different sense techniques, you actually realize you’ve been smelling this whole time but you didn’t really notice… You have the taste of coffee or whatever in your mouth… When you’re naming things, either saying them out loud or at least identifying them, what happens is a lot of people suddenly get pulled out of their thought loops. They didn’t realize they’d just been in this world of only thinking. Thinking is a sense, just like smelling and seeing, but I think we give it so much power. It’s the ultimate always-thinking sense. We get stuck in thinking and ignore the other senses. That’s where the thought loops and old patterns can take place when we’re stuck in just the thinking mode.

chapters.chapter_title: Yoga entry / Baron Baptiste / stimulus–response gap
chapters.excerpt: Cristine: Yeah. Mindfulness is a way into the present moment. It took me a while to get to meditation as a practice of stillness and silence. For me, my mind was so busy. The first thing I got to do was yoga. It was so divine — I knew it was God — because I had to be with people for almost a year to get it. I was supporting a woman in recovery. I would support her with principles, and then she would tell me, “Oh, you should go do yoga,” and she would ask me every week, “Have you done yoga?” By the time we’d worked together for several months I was like, “I have to go do yoga so I can at least answer yes.” So I got the book by Baron Baptiste, Journey Into Power, and that’s how I started. I didn’t go to a yoga studio — I just started at home.

chapters.chapter_title: Vipassana / Mahasati / fear that stillness = non-existence
chapters.excerpt: Cristine: Yes, for sure. I’m going to tell you about my whole journey with meditation. I did my yoga, got that down, and then I knew I was meant to explore Eastern meditation. My first glimpse at that was actually a movie called Doing Time, Doing Vipassana. Real meditation looked like Vipassana to me. That requires ten days of silence. There is a Vipassana retreat within distance from me that I could have done, but I was like, “I don’t know how I’d do that.” In the documentary it shows how Vipassana changed the nature of one of the worst prisons in the world in India. They brought it into the prison and it transformed the inmates — reduced the general issues, created better dynamics with the guards. It was really transformative. I thought that was so interesting. I did a teaching about principles around Eastern meditation on 11/11/11 at 11 a.m. I’m all about the numbers.

I hadn’t been able to get into silence and stillness, so he worked with me. He taught me Mahasati, which is a movement-based meditation — like a transition between yoga and meditation. Then we started talking about my deepest fears. I had this fear that if I were completely silent and still, it wasn’t safe. I associated it with non-existence. My deepest fear was that I would cease to exist, and the more still and silent I was, the more I felt like I fell into that fear. The doings and the act of motion was like a survival mechanism for me. My subconscious felt like I was alive and I existed as long as I was doing. Being wasn’t as safe, because at some level — and it has to do with that emptiness in me — it was like I would fall into the black hole of nothingness. I worked with him on that fear for a while, and through that I was able to grasp zero. When we talk about that neutrality, there is something beyond that on a quantum level that is actually the zero point field, where all energy is removed from a system. It is actually a ceasing of all. This thing that I was so afraid of, I actually had to move through it. In moving through it I found — and some of this was through quantum entrainment; Dr. Frank Kinslow is an advocate of this pure awareness — he talks about this transition from the zero point field to the unified field. There’s an amazing teacher of Transcendental Meditation that also talks about this: John Hagelin. John Hagelin is a quantum physicist who’s also a Transcendental Meditation teacher. He talks about the same kind of thing. There’s the dense 3D stuff, like a chair. Underneath that you’ve got molecular composition, then atomic, then subatomic, particles, the quantum weight… and when all of that’s gone, you’ve got the zero point field. But adjacent to the nothing is the everything, the all. In Buddhism that’s also a principle — the empty bowl, the Zen. If you take everything out, including ego, you have the potential for all, the vastness of Source to enter. I started to get this and recognize that that black hole fear was really just a tunnel to the everything, or a transition place. I actually created a technique, a meditation practice based on all this information, called Quantum Wholeness Meditation. Then I went to do TM. There’s a teacher here in Salt Lake. He mentioned that there are more billionaires than TM teachers, and I thought, isn’t that interesting? There’s only one in Utah. I felt really privileged to have that experience and learn about Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. I still am very much a fan. That led me to other solutions. I stuck with the 20 minutes twice a day for months, and then went back to Quantum Wholeness Meditation, partly because I do better and am more committed to it as a group practice. I’m one of those people that I’m going to do yoga if I go to yoga class and there’s other people in the room and somebody’s guiding me. I do meditation if I know it’s Monday at and we’re studying A Course in Miracles and doing meditation with intention together.

MBSR — mindfulness-based stress reduction — is kind of the same model as 20 minutes twice a day. People have adapted it, but it has become a huge part of our even academic models that support real solutions in mental health. So grateful for it. I think anybody would benefit from that, whether it’s a mantra or just mindfulness or whatever. You don’t forget your mantra. It is this loving thing — this personal word that doesn’t mean anything to anybody but you.
